item.text: {"winner":"B","confidence":"high","summary":"B is more faithful to the core contract: its FilesService.Upload uses the established multipart helper and delegates directly to Add, preserving Add’s behavior and option/error path. It needs unrelated scope removed and stronger tests, but A violates two explicit architectural requirements.","reasons":["B validates filename/content, calls multipartbody.NewFile(\"file\", fileName, content), and routes the result through FilesService.Add with opts unchanged.","A changes Add to eagerly buffer every caller-supplied body and wraps reader errors, altering the lower-level API’s existing streaming, memory, timing, and error semantics despite the contract requiring that behavior be preserved.","A’s Upload bypasses Add through a new private add method, contrary to the explicit requirement that Upload route through the existing Add method.","A has materially stronger upload tests: it verifies field name, filename, content, and multipart content on both retry attempts. B opens the uploaded part without reading its content, and its retry handler never verifies either request body, so it does not truly test payload replay integrity."],"risks_a":["The unrequested Add buffering can impose large memory costs on custom multipart callers and changes when source-reader failures occur.","Splitting request behavior into add weakens the required single-path design and could let Add and Upload semantics diverge later.","No visible tests cover Upload validation or source-reader failures."],"risks_b":["The new PersonsService.UploadPicture API and tests are unrelated scope and violate the instruction to add exactly the Files Upload convenience API.","Upload tests do not assert file content or that the streamed content is intact on both retry attempts.","No visible tests cover validation or source-reader failures."]}
